name: Ghostty
summary: A native, Zig-based terminal emulator and embeddable VT library that composes PTY processes, parser/screen state, GPU renderer backends, input routing, and configurable surface/runtime boundaries.
scope: terminal parser, screen, pages, and selection

features.name: PTY and child-process boundary
features.description: Each native-app Surface owns a PTY session. The Exec backend starts and stops the subprocess and supplies a PTY read thread to Termio; Surface separately owns terminal I/O and renderer thread managers. The application runtime decides whether a surface appears as a window, tab, or split. These native-app process responsibilities are distinct from the embeddable VT library.
benefits: Provides native shell execution with explicit PTY ownership
Keeps process lifecycle separate from terminal rendering state
costs: PTY and child behavior vary across supported operating systems
Each surface consumes process, file-descriptor, and buffer resources

features.name: Terminal parser, screen, and selection state
features.description: Ghostty separates terminal parsing, screen/page storage, cursor, selection, and protocol-specific state into reusable Zig modules, including a C-facing VT library surface.
benefits: Makes terminal emulation reusable by the native app and embeddable library
Supports explicit screen, page, selection, and parser state transitions
costs: Scrollback, images, and page storage consume memory
Protocol behavior and ABI-facing state require compatibility discipline

features.name: Renderer and graphics backend composition
features.description: Ghostty selects one graphics backend at compile time, Metal or OpenGL, for a shared generic renderer. Surface owns a renderer thread and shared renderer state; that state requires a mutex for access and includes demand-aware locking to prevent sustained PTY parsing from starving frame snapshots.
benefits: Supports native GPU backends while sharing terminal state
Separates renderer resources from terminal parser state
costs: Backend and driver capabilities differ by platform
GPU resources and frame scheduling affect latency and memory

features.name: Keyboard, mouse, paste, and event routing
features.description: Ghostty parses keyboard and mouse events, applies configurable bindings and paste policy, and routes resulting actions or encoded terminal input through surface and runtime event boundaries.
benefits: Makes terminal input and user actions explicit state transitions
Allows GUI events and terminal protocol input to share one surface model
costs: IME, keyboard layouts, and platform event semantics vary
Paste and input policy cross a user-interface/security boundary

features.name: Configuration, runtime, and surface authority
features.description: Ghostty configures terminal-program clipboard reads and writes separately: at this revision reads default to asking the user and writes to allow. Paste protection requests confirmation for potentially unsafe text, with bracketed paste treated as safe by default. Separate byte/line scrollback limits and an OSC 5522 clipboard-write byte limit bound retained data; these policies do not sandbox the child process.
benefits: Makes clipboard access and paste confirmation explicit policy decisions
Bounds retained scrollback and buffered clipboard transactions with configurable limits
costs: Allowing clipboard reads exposes host data to terminal programs
Relaxing resource limits trades bounded memory use for larger retained data

mathematical_views.question: How does child-process output transition through VT parsing and screen state into renderer frames and surface presentation?
assumptions: PTY output is ordered input to the parser
Screen/page state is the renderer input state
Frame scheduling and presentation are abstracted

mathematical_views.question: How do runtime windows or splits host surfaces that own PTY sessions, input state, and renderer resources?
assumptions: A surface is a lifecycle boundary
Terminal and renderer state are distinct resource classes
The model abstracts platform-specific GUI ownership

mathematical_views.question: Which terminal requests can read or write host clipboard data, and which retained buffers are constrained by configuration?
assumptions: Clipboard requests pass through configured allow, ask, or deny decisions
Resource limits bound selected retained buffers rather than total process memory
The relation explains policy and does not prove child-process isolation

benefits: Provides native shell execution with explicit PTY ownership
costs: PTY and child behavior vary across supported operating systems

benefits: Makes terminal emulation reusable by the native app and embeddable library
costs: Scrollback, images, and page storage consume memory

benefits: Supports native GPU backends while sharing terminal state
costs: Backend and driver capabilities differ by platform

benefits: Makes terminal input and user actions explicit state transitions
costs: IME, keyboard layouts, and platform event semantics vary
